Open the browser lab in a tab and leave it alone. R loads there in the background, so it will be ready long before you need it. ::: # PART 1 – Credibility and the toolchain {.darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 1 – 90 minutes ::: ::: notes Part one, then. A short opening on why any of this matters: the vocabulary that separates three kinds of repetition, and three very large studies that measured how often social-science findings survive being repeated, one of which supplies the case of today. Then the main business of the part, the toolchain, taken apart layer by layer: the language, the editor, the file formats, rendering, packages, version control, archives and licences. We finish on the two places where you will work today, the browser lab and the workspace, and on the setup check that gets your machine ready. ::: ## The data $\times$ analysis matrix ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](housing-one-day-data-tools_files/figure-revealjs/matrix-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.src} @AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen; @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms ::: ::: notes Here is the vocabulary of the course as a single grid, and if you take one thing home, make it this. The question stays the same throughout, and what varies is the data and the analysis. Same data and the same analysis is reproducibility: if I rerun your recipe, do I get your number? Same data but a different, justifiable analysis is robustness, which asks whether your finding survives my defensible choices. New data for the same question is replicability. The fourth cell, new data and new analysis, is really generalisation, and we leave it aside. Sit with the grid for a moment, because everything that follows refers back to it. ::: ## SCORE in brief {#score-in-brief .smaller} ::: {.fs-80} | Repetition | The study | What came back | |:-----|:-----|:-----| | **Reproduction** – same data, same analysis | 600 papers from 62 journals, 2009–2018 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial] | Of the 143 that could be assessed, **53.6%** reproduced precisely and **73.5%** at least approximately; counting the papers that nobody could check, about **18%** | | **Robustness** – same data, other analyses | Multi100: 100 studies, at least 5 analysts each [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] | **74%** of reanalyses reached the same conclusion; **34%** came within ±0.05 *d* of the original effect size | | **Replication** – new data | 274 claims, independent data [@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial] | **55.1%** significant again; the median effect size fell from *r* = 0.25 to 0.10 | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Measured on the same body of papers, the three are **essentially uncorrelated**: knowing how a finding fared on one tells you almost nothing about the others. ::: ::: notes SCORE, a programme funded by the research agency of the US Department of Defense, took a sample of social-science papers and put their central claims through each of the three repetitions on the grid. Reproduction first: of six hundred papers, the authors supplied data for about a quarter, and of the hundred and forty-three that could be assessed, about half reproduced precisely and three quarters approximately. Count the papers that nobody could check, and the rate is about eighteen per cent. Robustness was Multi100, where at least five analysts reanalysed each claim: three quarters reached the same conclusion, but only a third came close to the original effect size. Replication on new data: fifty-five per cent significant again, with effect sizes more than halved. [advance] And the three barely predict one another, so for any one paper you have to ask which of the three it passed. ::: ## What a Multi100 analyst received {#inside-multi100-what-an-analyst-was-sent .smaller} ::: {.small} - A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view - Its **central claim**, in one sentence, usually taken from the abstract - The **data**, or directions for fetching them - No instructions on method – any analysis you can defend ::: ::: {.fragment .small} And two things that no analyst was told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**. ::: ::: {.src} @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness. Registered protocol: osf.io/dy68c ::: ::: notes Multi100 handed a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each, and I was one of those analysts, on a different paper from the one we work on today. Let me describe what that was like from the inside, because it shapes how you read the results. What arrived was the published paper, the whole thing and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view, and if anything that pulls you towards the original answer. With it came the central claim of the paper in a single sentence, usually taken from the abstract, and the data or directions for fetching them. What did not arrive was any instruction on method: analyse it however you can defend. And two things stayed hidden throughout, who the other analysts were and what any of them were finding. The isolation was part of the design, because it is what makes the spread at the end mean something. ::: ## The two Multi100 tasks {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller} ::: {.small} **Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. ::: ::: {.fragment .small} **Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, instructions arrived: report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests (or an alternative or non-parametric version), with an instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis. ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged. ::: ::: notes The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion out of four, evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived. It asked for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, and it came with a short instruction for each claim that pinned down one or two details of the analysis. [advance] The order matters because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number, and that question can only be asked once everyone is answering roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for. We will read the instruction for our own claim later. ::: ## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller} ::: {.small} - Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size - Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis - A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim - Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts. ::: ::: notes Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms. Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. Multi100 converted those onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on the same axis. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all, so the spread that comes out of the study is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted. One is that they estimate the same quantity, and a good deal of what follows is about what happens when they do not. The other is that each conversion counts the units that actually carry the evidence. ::: ## Open-source software {#what-open-source-buys-you .smaller} ::: {.small} - **You can read it.** The source of `lm()`, of `glm()`, of every package that this course loads, is public, so no estimator has to be taken on trust - **No licence stands between a reader and your analysis.** Anyone, anywhere, can run your code without buying anything - **It outlives your institution.** A licence expires when you change job; a package on CRAN does not - **You can fix it, and so can others.** Bugs get found because thousands of people run the same code on different data ::: ::: {.fragment .small} With a proprietary toolchain, **the price of reproducing your work falls on your reader**, who has to buy the licence. ::: ::: notes Stata is proprietary and R is open source, and that difference matters for reproduction. There are four reasons, and only one of them is money. First, you can read it. You can go and look at the source of any function we run in this course, so you never have to take an estimator on trust. Second, and this is the one that bears on our subject, no licence stands between a reader and your analysis. If your replication package needs a licence they do not have, your work is not reproducible for them, however carefully you wrote it. Third, it outlives your institution – a site licence ends when you change job, and a package on CRAN does not. Fourth, bugs get found, because thousands of people run the same code against different data. On money, the question is who pays. Reproducibility has a price, and a proprietary toolchain hands that price to your reader. ::: ## The toolchain {#the-toolchain-laid-out .smaller} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}

The others are there so that you know what you are choosing between. ::: ::: notes The whole set of tools fits on one slide once you sort it by job rather than by brand family. First, something to analyse with – R, which is what we use, but Python and Julia are entirely reasonable choices for this work, and Stata and SPSS are still the default in a lot of departments. Second, somewhere to write it: Positron is what I will be driving on the shared screen, RStudio is the one that most of you will already know, VS Code does everything if you are willing to configure it, Jupyter is the notebook world. Quarto turns text and code into a document; git records every version with a date; GitHub hosts the repository so others can reach it; and OSF or Zenodo give the whole thing a permanent address with a DOI. Ringed in orange is what this course uses, and the rest is there so you know the alternatives. ::: ## Programming languages {#languages-what-you-are-actually-choosing .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
RBuilt by statisticians for data analysis. Hard to beat for models, tables and figures, thanks to its packages.
PythonA general language that also does data. Better for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning.
JuliaFast, young, small ecosystem. Worth it when your model takes hours.
StataExcellent panel and survey estimators, superb docs, one syntax. Costs money and hides its source.
::: ::: {.fragment .small} You do not have to choose once and forever. Quarto runs R, Python and Julia chunks in the **same document**, and the course browser lab is R compiled to run inside a web page. ::: ::: notes A slower look at the languages, because people agonise about this and mostly should not. R was built by statisticians for data analysis, and that is still where it wins, in models, tables and figures. Most of that comes from the package ecosystem: whatever obscure estimator your literature uses, someone has written the package. Python is a general-purpose language that also does data, so it is the better choice for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning. Julia is fast and young with a small ecosystem, and earns its place when a model takes hours rather than seconds. Stata deserves respect – excellent panel and survey estimators, the best documentation in the business, one consistent syntax – and it costs money and hides its source. And none of this is a life choice, because Quarto will run R, Python and Julia chunks in the same document. ::: ## Editors and IDEs {#where-you-write-it .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 5"}
PositronThe newer IDE from Posit. R and Python as equals, VS Code underneath.
RStudioStill excellent, still supported. If it is what you know, use it.
VS CodeDoes anything, once configured. Big extension ecosystem.
JupyterNotebook-first. Beware: cells can run out of order.
NeovimFor the keyboard-only. Steep to learn, and very fast once learned.
::: ::: {.fragment .small} Of the choices in the toolchain, the editor matters least. It changes how *you* work and nothing about what a reader receives. **A trap:** a notebook lets you run cells out of order, so it can show output that no clean run would produce. Restart and run everything before you believe it. ::: ::: {.src} Positron and RStudio are both from Posit; both are free, and RStudio is open source. ::: ::: notes The editor is the least consequential choice in the toolchain, so I will be quick. Positron is the newer environment from Posit, built on VS Code, treating R and Python as equals – it is what I will be driving on the shared screen. RStudio is still excellent and still supported, and if it is what you know, there is no reason to move. VS Code will do anything once you have configured it. Jupyter is notebook-first and Python-first. Neovim is for people who never want to touch a mouse. What matters is the trap in the second box, and it applies to every notebook-style tool including the interactive mode in Quarto: you can run cells out of order, which means the output on your screen may be output that no clean run would ever produce. Restart the session and run everything, top to bottom, before you believe a number. ::: ## Plain-text file formats {#plain-text-is-the-format-that-survives .smaller} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
.RCode only, with prose in comments.
.mdProse only. Headings, lists, links – no code.
.RmdProse + R, rendered together. R only.
.qmdProse + R, Python or Julia. The course format.
::: ::: {.fragment .small} Every one of these is a **plain text file**. You can open it in anything, compare two versions of it line by line, email it, and read it in twenty years. A `.docx` with pasted output is not plain text, and nothing in it records which numbers came from which code. ::: ::: notes Four file types, in increasing order of what they hold. A dot-R file is code with comments. A markdown file is prose with no code. An R Markdown file is prose and R together, rendered into one document. And a Quarto file is the same idea, except the code can be R or Python or Julia. What they have in common is that every one is a plain text file. You can open it in any editor, see exactly what changed between two versions, email it, and still read it in twenty years. Compare that with a Word document holding numbers you pasted in from somewhere. It looks the same on the page, but nothing in it records which number came from which line of code. That is how the old value of a number you have since recomputed can still be sitting in the paper. ::: ## What happens when you render {#how-a-document-becomes-a-document} ![](pics/tools/render-pipeline.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"} ::: {.small} You write **one** source file. Rendering runs your code, inserts the results, and produces whatever output you asked for from that one source. ::: ::: notes And this is what happens when you press render. You write one source file, with prose and code together. Knitr – or Jupyter, if you are working in Python – runs every chunk of code in a fresh session and replaces it with its actual output, giving a plain markdown file. Pandoc then turns that into whatever you asked for: a Word document for your co-author, a PDF for the journal, a web page for your project site, slides like these. So there is one place where a number is computed, and every output shows the same number, because they were all produced from the same source in the same run. When a reviewer asks you to drop three countries, you change one line and re-render, and the table, the figure and the sentence in the text all change together. That alone makes rendering worth learning, quite apart from anything to do with credibility. ::: ## The package layer {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
easystatsData work with datawizard, and model output as tidy data: parameters, performance, effect sizes.
tidyverseReading files, and the verbs that datawizard lacks. One grammar across all of it.
modelsummaryRegression tables you can publish, from the fitted objects.
marginaleffectsPredictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model.
::: ::: {.fragment .small} Your figures come from **`tinyplot`**, and the answers about causal graphs from **`dagitty`**, which cannot run in the browser labs, so they print the answers that it gave for the graphs of each task. The setup page lists the full set, and the check script in your workspace reports anything that is missing. ::: ::: notes A word about packages, because this is where the advantage of R actually lies. Easystats comes first in this course. Its datawizard package does the data work, filtering, selecting and summarising, and the rest of the family turns model output back into tidy data – coefficients, fit statistics, effect sizes – instead of the printed blob that summary gives you. The tidyverse reads the files and covers the few verbs that datawizard lacks. Modelsummary builds publication-ready regression tables straight from fitted model objects, so your table cannot disagree with your model. And marginaleffects computes predictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model you can fit, which is how you get from a coefficient to a statement in the units that your reader thinks in. The figures that you draw come from tinyplot and the causal graphs from dagitty, and the check script in your workspace reports anything that is missing. ::: ## Version control {#version-control-in-one-slide .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.small} **Git** is a program on your machine. It records a **complete, dated snapshot** every time you say so, and it never forgets one. **GitHub** is a website that hosts those snapshots so other people can reach them – and it is not the only one (GitLab, Codeberg, one hosted by your university). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.small} What it gives you that a folder of `final_v3_REALLY_final.R` cannot: - Every past state, recoverable exactly - A written reason attached to each change - A public, timestamped trail of when you knew what - A way for two people to edit the same file without one overwriting the other ::: ::: :::: ::: {.fragment .small} The tasks use **none of it**. There is a companion module on the site, and your workspace folder is the ideal thing to practise on. ::: ::: notes Version control is the one tool that I have kept out of the tasks, so let me at least name it properly. Git is a program that runs on your machine: every time you tell it to, it records a complete dated snapshot of your project, and it never forgets one. GitHub is a website that hosts those snapshots so other people can reach them. It is not the only one: there is GitLab, there is Codeberg, and your university may run its own. What does that give you that a folder full of final-version-three-really-final does not? Every past state recoverable exactly, a written reason attached to every change, a public timestamped trail of when you knew what – which, notice, is a preregistration mechanism in itself – and a way for two people to work on one file without one silently overwriting the other. There is a companion module on the site. ::: ## Where data and code are archived {#where-data-and-code-go-to-live .smaller} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
OSFProjects, files, and registrations. Free, and it hosts the public records of SCORE and Multi100.
ZenodoCERN-run archive. Gives a DOI; takes a GitHub release directly.
DataverseInstitutional data archives with proper metadata and curation.
XYZDomain archivesGESIS, UK Data Service, ICPSR – licensed access to survey microdata.
::: ::: {.fragment .small} **A repository is not an archive.** A GitHub repository can have its history rewritten, be renamed, or be deleted tomorrow. An archived deposit gets a **DOI**, a fixed version, and a commitment to keep serving it. Serious work usually needs both. ::: ::: notes And the last group: where things go so they are still there in ten years. OSF is free, holds projects and files and registrations, and the public records of SCORE and Multi100 are kept there – you will read some of them later. Zenodo is run by CERN, gives you a DOI, and will take a GitHub release directly, which makes archiving a one-click habit. Dataverse is the institutional data-archive world with proper metadata and curation. And then the domain archives – GESIS, the UK Data Service, ICPSR – which is where licensed survey microdata is held. A repository is not an archive, although people often treat it as one. A GitHub repository can have its history rewritten, be renamed or be deleted tomorrow, and the link in your paper dies. An archived deposit has a DOI, a fixed version and an institution committed to serving it. Serious work usually needs both. ::: ## Licences, briefly {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ::: {.small} | What | Common choice | Why | |---|---|---| | **Code** | MIT or GPL | MIT: use it however you like. GPL: and share your changes back | | **Data** | CC0 or CC BY | CC0 puts it in the public domain; CC BY asks for attribution | | **Text, figures, slides** | CC BY or CC BY-NC | Attribution, optionally no commercial reuse | | **Someone else's data** | *their* terms | Licensed survey microdata usually may not be passed on, by me or by you | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Publishing with no licence is not a neutral default. It means **all rights reserved** – legally, nobody may reuse the work at all. ::: ::: notes Licensing gets skipped and then bites. Four rows. For code, MIT says use it however you like, GPL says use it and share your changes back. For data, CC-zero puts it in the public domain and CC-BY asks for attribution. For text and figures and slides, CC-BY or CC-BY with a non-commercial clause. And the fourth row is the one that most often constrains a reanalysis: when the data are not yours, their terms govern. Much survey microdata is held under a licence that lets you analyse it and forbids you to pass it on, so a replication package can carry the code and point to the archive, but not the file itself. A dataset released under CC-zero, by contrast, can travel with the code, and anyone can rerun the analysis without asking anyone. And the line at the bottom: leaving a repository without a licence does not make it free to use. Legally it means all rights reserved, so nobody may reuse it at all. ::: ## The browser lab and the workspace {#what-we-use-today .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.small} **The browser lab** - One web page, with R compiled to run **inside the browser** - Nothing installed, and the data already in place - Every task of the day, with the same helpers as the workspace - What I drive on the shared screen ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.small} **The workspace, if you have installed R** - The folder that you downloaded, opened in your IDE - Quarto renders your report, and R fits every model in a moment - No git, no cloning, no configuration – it is just files - What you keep after the day ::: ::: :::: ::: {.urlbox .fragment} [https://github.com/CodeMoreh/replication-lab-housing](https://github.com/CodeMoreh/replication-lab-housing)
[download the zip → unzip → open in your IDE]{.fs-60} ::: ::: notes Two places to work, with the same tasks and the same numbers. The browser lab is one web page with R compiled to run inside the browser itself: nothing to install, nothing to break, and the data are already there. It is what I drive on the shared screen, and it is where most of you will work today. The workspace is the folder that you can download and open in your IDE, which is Positron on my screen and may be RStudio or VS Code on yours. Quarto renders the report, R fits every model live, and there is no git and no cloning, because it is just a folder of files. "n_emails gets 1014" mean(c(1, 0, 1, 1)) # a function: name, then arguments in () audit$reply # $ picks one column out of a data frame audit |> nrow() # |> the pipe: send the left into the right ``` ::: {.small} With four pieces of syntax you can read most R: **assign** with `<-`, **call** a function with `name(...)`, **reach into** an object with `$`, and **chain** with the pipe `|>`. ::: ::: notes If you have never written a line of R, this slide is most of what you need to read the rest. Four things. First, the arrow assigns: n emails gets one thousand and fourteen. You will see the equals sign used the same way and both work, but the arrow is the convention. Second, a function is a name followed by round brackets holding its arguments: the mean of one, nought, one and one, which is three quarters, and which is also how you get a share out of a column of zeros and ones. Third, the dollar sign reaches inside a data frame to pull out one column. And fourth, the pipe takes whatever is on its left and feeds it in as the first argument of whatever is on its right. Read it as the word "then", and long chains become sentences. ::: ## Getting data in {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3"} audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv") # read it, name it audit # print it ``` ::: {.small} What comes back is a **data frame**: a rectangle with one row per observation, here one email, and one column per variable, each column of a single type. `readr::` names the package that the function comes from. The package must be installed first; that happens once, and the setup page says how. ::: ::: notes Getting data in. The part before the double colon names the package that the function comes from, here readr, so that you can always see where a function lives; the package has to be installed first, which is a separate step that you do once. Then read underscore csv reads the file and the arrow gives the result a name, so from here on audit is our data. Typing the name on its own prints it. What you get back is a data frame, the central object of R: a rectangle with one row for each email and one column for each variable, every column holding a single type. Nearly every function that you will meet takes a data frame and hands one back, which is why the pipe works so well: the output of one step is the right shape to be the input of the next. ::: ## Inspecting the data {#look-before-you-model .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2|3|4"} datawizard::data_peek(audit) # every column, its type, the first few values nrow(audit) # 1014 datawizard::data_tabulate(audit$name) # how many emails went out under each name? datawizard::data_tabulate(audit$reply) # 1, 0 – and NA for the emails that bounced ``` ::: {.fragment .small} `NA` is how R marks a missing value. Here it means that an email bounced and never reached anyone, which is a different thing from an email that drew no reply. Most serious errors are visible in the data before they reach a model. ::: ::: notes With the data loaded, look at them before any model touches them. Data peek shows every column with its type and its first few values. nrow counts the rows, one per email. Data tabulate tells you how many emails went out under each name, which should be roughly equal, because the names were assigned at random. And tabulating the reply column gives you ones, zeros, and a handful of NA. [advance] NA is how R marks a missing value, and in this file it means something specific: the email bounced and never reached an official. That is not the same as an email that drew no reply, and a model that treated the two alike would be measuring a failure of delivery. Every serious error I have made was visible in the data before it reached a model. ::: ## Working with rows and columns {#five-verbs-do-most-of-the-work .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ```{.r code-line-numbers="|2|3|4|5"} audit |> datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1 & !is.na(named)) |> # keep the coded replies datawizard::data_select(c("name", "group", "named")) |> # keep three columns datawizard::data_modify(hispanic = group == "hispanic") |> # make a new column datawizard::data_arrange("name") # sort ``` ::: {.fragment .small} The fifth verb is `data_summary()`, here with `by`: collapse many rows into one per group. ```{.r} audit |> datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1 & !is.na(named)) |> datawizard::data_summary(replies = n(), greeted = mean(named), by = "group") ``` ::: ::: notes Four verbs get you a very long way, and they share one pattern: a data frame goes in and a data frame comes out. Data filter keeps rows, here the replies that carry a greeting code. Data select keeps columns. Data modify makes a new column, here a true or false for the Hispanic names. Data arrange sorts. All four come from datawizard, the package of the course for data work. Read it downwards as a sentence: take the emails, then keep the coded replies, then keep three columns, then add a column, then sort by name. [advance] The fifth verb is data summary, which collapses many rows into one per group. These three lines give you, for each group of names, the number of coded replies and the share that greeted the sender by name: the right-hand panel of the figure that you met earlier, as a table. ::: ## Tables and tests {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-3|5|6"} coded_replies <- original |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |> datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup)) tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies) chisq.test(tab_8ptrz) ``` ::: {.small} `xtabs()` counts the rows in each combination of two variables, a **cross-tabulation**. `chisq.test()` asks whether the two variables are independent in the table. The first block reads the public file of the original authors, keeps the replies that carry a greeting code, and makes a true or false column for the Hispanic names, using grepl, which asks whether a piece of text matches a pattern; the little hat means "starts with". Then xtabs counts the replies in each combination of two variables, Hispanic name or not and greeted by name or not, which gives a two-by-two table. And chisq dot test asks whether the two variables are independent in that table. That is the whole reproduction of one of the five analysts, 8PTRZ, and the other four put a model or a test of two proportions in place of the table. When you get there, look at the first line of what it prints, because it names something that matters. ::: ## Model formulas {#a-model-is-a-formula-plus-data .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5"} named ~ hispanic # "named explained by hispanic" m <- lm(named ~ hispanic, data = replies) # a linear model g <- glm(named ~ hispanic, family = binomial(), data = replies) # a logit ``` ::: {.small} The tilde `~` reads **outcome on the left, predictors on the right**; add predictors with `+`. Almost every modelling function in R has this shape: `something(formula, data = ...)`. ::: ::: {.fragment .small} With a 0/1 outcome and a 0/1 predictor, the coefficient of `lm()` **is** the difference between the two shares. Part 3 comes back to both models[, in the reproduction]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.menu"}. ::: ::: notes A model in R is a formula plus data, and the tilde is the heart of the formula: outcome on the left, predictors on the right, more predictors added with a plus. Then lm fits a linear model, and glm with the binomial family fits a logistic regression, a logit. Almost every modelling function in R has this same shape, a formula and then data, so once you know it, lm, glm and everything after them become variations on one pattern. [advance] And one fact that makes this case easy to learn on: when the outcome is zero or one and the predictor is zero or one, the coefficient of the linear model is exactly the difference between the two shares. We come back to both models in Part 3[, when you reproduce the analysts]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.menu"}. ::: ## Plotting with tinyplot {#one-line-of-ggplot .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-3|4|5"} greeted <- audit |> datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1 & !is.na(named)) |> datawizard::data_summary(greeted = mean(named), by = c("name", "group")) tinyplot::tinyplot(greeted ~ name | group, data = greeted, # what goes where, coloured by group type = "p", flip = TRUE) # draw points, names on the side ``` ::: {.small} Two parts: a **formula**, `y ~ x | group`, with the **data**, which says what goes on which axis and what sets the colour, and a **type** that says what to draw. ::: ::: notes Plotting, briefly, with tinyplot, the package that draws every figure of your workspace and of the browser lab. First the data: the share of coded replies that greeted the sender by name, for each of the six names, kept in a small table called greeted. Then a tinyplot has two parts. A formula with the data, the same tilde as in a model, which says what goes on which axis, and the vertical bar adds a third variable that sets the colour, here the group that the name was meant to indicate. And a type, which says what to draw: points. Flip turns the chart on its side, so the names can be read. The plot it makes is a rough version of the right-hand panel from earlier. ::: ## Causal graphs in R {#a-causal-graph-is-a-set-of-arrows .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ```{.r code-line-numbers="|2|3|4-5|6|10|11"} dag <- make_dag( "name -> reply", "reply -> greeting", "official -> reply", "official -> greeting", "community -> reply", "community -> greeting", # "name -> greeting", # the arrow that the claim is about exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official" ) dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag) # what must be adjusted for? dagitty::paths(dag, Z = "reply") # which paths open among the replies? ``` ::: {.small} One arrow per line, written **cause -> effect**, so a `#` takes an arrow out and the code still runs. `make_dag()` is a helper of the workspace, built on **dagitty**. ::: ::: notes [The last piece of R is the one you use in the next task.]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.data-tools"}[The last piece of R is one that the other formats of the course use for the causal graph of the experiment, so I take it quickly.]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.data-tools"} A causal graph in the workspace is a list of arrows, one per line, written cause, then an arrow, then effect. The name points at the reply, the reply at the greeting, and the official and the community each point at both. The arrow that the claim is about is commented out with a hash, so that you decide whether to switch it on. You also declare which node is the exposure, which the outcome, and that the official is latent, unobserved. Then two questions for dagitty. adjustmentSets asks what you must adjust for to estimate the effect of the name, and paths, with Z set to the reply, asks which paths between the name and the greeting are open once the comparison is made among the replies. ::: ## Common error messages {#when-it-breaks .smaller .deepdive run="tools"} ::: {.small} | What you see | What it usually means | |---|---| | `could not find function "try_spec"` | The helpers are not loaded – run `source("R/spec_tools.R")` | | `object 'audit' not found` | You ran this chunk before the one that creates it – go back up and run in order | | `object 'hispanic_name' not found` | The column does not exist yet – you skipped the `data_modify()` that makes it | | `+` on the console, nothing happens | An unclosed bracket or quote.
